questions.question: What is a cache hit?
options: Accessing data that is already in cache, so it is faster
Accessing data that is not in memory at all
A cryptographic collision in a hash function
A CPU exception caused by invalid memory
questions.explanation: A cache hit means the requested line is present in the cache, so access is fast.

questions.question: What does a Prime+Probe attacker try to infer?
options: Which cache sets/lines the victim accessed, by measuring evictions
The victim’s source code from binary output
The victim’s network address via DNS
The victim’s random number generator seed from ciphertext length
questions.explanation: Prime+Probe infers cache activity by priming and then probing for misses.

questions.question: Which step order matches Prime+Probe?
options: Prime cache → victim runs → probe cache timings
Flush cache → victim runs → reload shared line
Encrypt message → compare digests → decrypt message
Train branch predictor → read registers → dump memory
questions.explanation: Prime+Probe is prime, victim, probe (measure which accesses got slower).

questions.question: Why can a secret-dependent table lookup leak information in caches?
options: Different indices touch different cache sets/lines, changing later access times
Because table lookups always reveal the secret directly
Because caches store cryptographic keys in plaintext
Because AES requires cache flushing after each round
questions.explanation: Memory access patterns influence cache state, which can be measured indirectly.

questions.question: What makes Flush+Reload different from Prime+Probe?
options: Flush+Reload requires shared memory pages between attacker and victim
Flush+Reload works only against symmetric cryptography
Prime+Probe requires shared memory pages between attacker and victim
Prime+Probe can only be done remotely
questions.explanation: Flush+Reload typically relies on shared pages; Prime+Probe does not.

questions.question: Which mitigation most directly targets cache side-channel leakage in crypto code?
options: Use constant-time, table-free implementations for secret-dependent operations
Increase ciphertext length
Compress network responses
Add random whitespace to JSON outputs
questions.explanation: The root cause is secret-dependent memory access; constant-time/table-free code addresses it.

questions.question: Why are “random delays” not a strong mitigation for cache/timing attacks?
options: Attackers can average out noise across many measurements
Random delays change the cache associativity
Random delays disable branch prediction permanently
Random delays prevent the victim from accessing memory
questions.explanation: Noise reduces signal quality but often doesn’t eliminate it statistically.

questions.question: In a direct-mapped cache, what causes a conflict miss?
options: Two different addresses map to the same set, so one evicts the other
A hash collision in the address computation
A CPU timer overflow
A mismatch in MAC verification
questions.explanation: Direct-mapped caches have one line per set; different tags mapping to the same set conflict.
